entries.title: DHS head Markwayne Mullin says there is not a threat to the U.S. amid FAA ground stop
entries.summary: Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin spoke to at the White House on Friday afternoon after the FAA issues a total ground stop. NPR was there for the briefing.
entries.content:
DHS head Markwayne Mullin says there is not a threat to the U.S. amid FAA ground stop

Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin spoke to at the White House on Friday afternoon after the FAA issues a total ground stop. NPR was there for the briefing.

SACHA PFEIFFER, HOST:

Travelers across the country are now stranded in airports and sitting on runways after the FAA issued a total ground stop this afternoon. There are very few details about why Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy made that call. All we know at this time is that it's being attributed to communication difficulties. Here is Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin speaking at the White House just a few minutes ago.

(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)

MARKWAYNE MULLIN: We're getting a ton of calls saying, is this a terrorist attack? Is this a terrorist attack? Everybody's safe. There is no reason to be concerned about your loved ones, if they're flying or anything like that. I just want to make sure everybody's at ease about that.

PFEIFFER: NPR White House correspondent Deepa Shivaram was there listening to Mullin when he talked to reporters, and she's with us now. Deepa, what can you tell us about what's going on?

DEEPA SHIVARAM, BYLINE: Yeah. So this all happened in the span of the last 30 minutes, I would say. DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin came out to brief reporters just outside the White House, and he started off by saying that there is not a threat to the U.S., and they believe that this whole situation boils down to a telecommunications issue.

(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)

MULLIN: There was no prior indication. There was no indication as of yet that this was a nefarious attack against us. It is just a telecommunication outage as of right now.

SHIVARAM: He was asked about his wording there, as of yet, when he said that there, you know, wasn't any indication that this was a nefarious attack. He said that they're not ruling out anything. They're still looking into the details, and they're not at a point where they can rule anything out, hence his wording, as of yet. He said that all flights are accounted for, and he was very emphatic multiple times that this was not a 9/11 situation.

MULLIN: Out of abundance of caution, we have grounded all the flights, and all the flights are accounted for. As incoming flights, either internationally or the flights that are currently still in the air - we'll be dealing with those case by case.

SHIVARAM: The secretary also said that he does not think this is affecting other countries. He did have some information that was a little unclear, though. He added that there are two places in the U.S. that were not affected by this outage, this communications outage, but he couldn't quite share more details about that. So that part of this is a little bit unclear and, I think, underscores that there's still a lot of information that's coming in.

PFEIFFER: Interesting. I guess we'll find out later whether he means continental U.S. or otherwise. We'll try to answer that question for our listeners later. Did he give any details about what steps are underway to try to resolve this?

SHIVARAM: Yeah. So he said the first thing officials are working on is trying to restore communications to the full extent, make sure that all flights are on the ground. But no specific timeline was given here, Sacha. He was asked if this whole process was going to be, you know, a matter hours. Are people going to be stuck on tarmacs? Is it going to take days, months? He didn't really have an exact answer to that. All he said is that it's going to take some time. And he said this isn't going to be turned around within the hour. It's just going to take some time, and that part is still a little bit unclear as well.

PFEIFFER: Deepa, as I've been reading about this over the past 30 minutes, I saw some reporting that said there was some new system, possibly an AI-driven system, that was rolled out earlier this week by the FAA. Do you know anything?

SHIVARAM: Yeah. So at at this stage, the secretary said that this outage today is not connected to this AI system, and I'll just explain that really quickly. The FAA rolled out an AI air traffic tool nationwide earlier this week, and that tool is built to help assist with air traffic management. It was already piloted in D.C., actually, in September, and then this week, it was applied nationwide. The secretary said, though, that at this stage, they don't think those two things are connected. He also was asked about the Microsoft outage that happened yesterday and if there was any possible connection to that and what's going on today. And he said he didn't see any reason to connect those two situations.

PFEIFFER: Has President Trump weighed in on this at all?

SHIVARAM: We have not heard from the president yet. I have been refreshing his social media feed to try and see if we will hear from him imminently. He has been briefed on this, and the secretary said that, you know, everybody's involved with this right now. It takes the FAA, obviously. The transportation secretary, Sean Duffy, has been speaking with the president, the State Department. He called the situation unprecedented when you have something like this going on. I will say, in terms of Trump's travel plans, he is expected to stay in Washington this weekend, so no imminent travel for him, but he is planning on Monday to depart for Asia, where he'll be going to the Philippines and China for two summits.

PFEIFFER: You know, Deepa, I am supposed to fly tonight. I'm now bracing...

SHIVARAM: Oh.

PFEIFFER: ...Myself for probably not being...

SHIVARAM: My goodness.

PFEIFFER: ...Able to fly tonight. So I have so many questions. And I have a few I want to ask you that you actually may not know. Please feel free to say, I don't know.

SHIVARAM: Yeah.

PFEIFFER: We know they're grounded, and you touched on this, but do we know if planes that are actually in the air are going to be brought down, they have to get out of the air? Or that's a case-by-case situation?

SHIVARAM: Yeah. So that's, like, kind of a split ticket right now. The secretary did say that they're working on getting all flights grounded. So I think that's something that's in the process of happening. The split ticket that I referred to, I think, when it comes to international flights that are incoming - that is being treated as a case-by-case basis.

PFEIFFER: And in terms of where the planes who might have to come down quickly have to go, that's...

SHIVARAM: Yeah.

PFEIFFER: ...Just the challenge that air traffic controllers deal with. How do we get them down? Where do we put them?

SHIVARAM: Yes. So when they talk about this communications outage, I believe that the secretary said they're still able to communicate with certain planes that are in the air and things like that. And so the process of getting everybody on the ground sounds like it's obviously very complicated. The specifics on which communications elements here are, you know, up in the air, for lack of a better word and unclear - that part is sort of just broadly being spoken as a widespread telecommunications issue.

PFEIFFER: So I imagine a lot of people stuck in airports, a lot stuck in tarmacs. If people are trying to decide whether to go to the airport, maybe call your airline, but I'm sure they're overwhelmed by calls right now.

SHIVARAM: Yes. It sounds like the information is a little unclear, especially when it comes to grounding flights versus departing flights. I don't think there's been guidance that's been issued on that quite yet.

PFEIFFER: Thank you for that. That's NPR White House correspondent Deepa Shivaram.

SHIVARAM: Thank you.

entries.title: Stuck on the tarmac without information: Travelers share their ground stop experiences
entries.summary: Passengers stuck on airplanes on tarmacs across the country during the FAA ground stop on Friday share their stories.
entries.content:
Stuck on the tarmac without information: Travelers share their ground stop experiences

Passengers stuck on airplanes on tarmacs across the country during the FAA ground stop on Friday share their stories.

SCOTT DETROW, HOST:

When today's FAA ground stop was announced, thousands of planes at airports across the country were on the tarmac with passengers on board. We spoke with one of them, Regina Heirlig (ph).

REGINA HEIRLIG: I am at the Dallas Fort Worth airport right now, and I'm trying to go to San Diego. I flew out of BWI in Baltimore this morning and connecting in Dallas Fort Worth, trying to go to San Diego. I'm trying to help a family member who had an emergency, and so I need to get there, and I hope it's today, but I'm not feeling really optimistic about it at this point.

SACHA PFEIFFER, HOST:

We also heard from Gillian Karen (ph).

GILLIAN KAREN: I'm at O'Hare, and I'm going to LaGuardia. We boarded normal time, everything normal, sat on the tarmac for quite some time. And then flight attendant comes over the speaker saying there's a nationwide grounding.

DETROW: Allison Frankel (ph) said she was in a bit of an information vacuum.

ALLISON FRANKEL: You know, it's hard sitting here without information, so we're all looking for information and guidance from the government and for as much information as we can from news reporters. But at the end of the day, you know, we all want to stay safe, so grateful, at least, to be on the ground and safe.

PFEIFFER: And as we were talking to Gillian Karen, she got some news.

KAREN: Oh, wait, sorry. There's - hold on, they're...

UNIDENTIFIED PERSON: (Inaudible). Turn off seatbelts.

KAREN: Oh, OK. We are at the gate.

DETROW: Good news - better to be in the terminal than on the tarmac all night.

entries.title: What we know about the FAA nationwide ground stop
entries.summary: The Federal Aviation Administration took an extraordinary step Friday afternoon by issuing a nationwide ground stop. No planes are taking off at any airport and millions of passengers are stranded.
entries.content:
What we know about the FAA nationwide ground stop

The Federal Aviation Administration took an extraordinary step Friday afternoon by issuing a nationwide ground stop. No planes are taking off at any airport and millions of passengers are stranded.

SCOTT DETROW, HOST:

The U.S. air travel system is slowly getting back off the ground. The Federal Aviation Administration has lifted the rare nationwide ground stop it issued earlier today, citing telecommunications failure. That grounded thousands of planes at airports across the country, stranding millions of passengers. NPR's transportation correspondent Joel Rose is here. We've been talking all afternoon and evening trying to sort this out. Joel, now we have a little bit of a resolution, but not really. What's the latest?

JOEL ROSE, BYLINE: Yeah. We just heard from the transportation secretary, Sean Duffy, that, as you said, the airspace has reopened. The ground stop is lifted. But it's going to take some time to get this hourslong - to get through the backlog of canceled and delayed flights. And it's going to take even longer to figure out, apparently, what happened here.

During the news conference, Duffy said that investigators are still trying to understand exactly what the problem was. Duffy blamed the - Duffy cited intermittent communications, intermittent radar and blamed this on outdated air traffic control equipment that was overloaded with data. We have old switches, old routers, he said. It's an old system that went down. It got overloaded. Here's more of what Duffy said.

(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)

UNIDENTIFIED PERSON: We're getting very little information. Our pilot's been great and has been giving us updates every 15 minutes, which has been really helpful and reassuring.

DETROW: I think we had the wrong tape there, Joel. But...

ROSE: That's the wrong cut. Well, you got...

DETROW: Yeah, yeah, keep going.

ROSE: I'll tell you more about Secretary Duffy.

DETROW: Sure.

ROSE: So he spent a lot of this press conference blaming old gear that failed. But when reporters pushed and asked for clarity on exactly what went wrong today, he wasn't able to give them a whole lot of specifics. He pivoted again and again to pushing for more money to rebuild the nation's air traffic control system, which has been a big priority for this administration but was - we just don't - we still have only Duffy's word that this was the old gear that failed. We don't have a lot of detail on what it was.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin was at this press conference too. He said, there's no indication that this was a cyber attack, but he could not rule that out entirely - also started the press conference by saying that this outage is not related to the Microsoft outage that knocked out Outlook and some other services yesterday.

DETROW: Yeah, I feel like I had a lot of questions watching that briefing, as did many other people. And meanwhile, there's people all over the country trying to get home. Our reporter at Washington National Airport, Ava Berger, says she is hearing announcements that the hold's has been lifted, but the announcements are saying - urging people to please be patient. About half the board there is red with canceled flights. But she said people are now starting to optimistically slowly go back to their gates to see if their plane's ever going to leave. I mean, Joel, what is the situation like on the ground at other airports around the country?

ROSE: This is a mess, and it's going to be a mess for days. I mean, we've canceled - airlines have canceled thousands of flights. Thousands more are delayed. Planes are out of position. Crews are out of position. This is, you know, imagine if you had a giant blizzard at every airport in the country all at once.

DETROW: Ooh.

ROSE: You know, it's like the whole system is scrambled, and it's going to take days, optimistically...

DETROW: Yeah.

ROSE: ...Before we are back to normal in the U.S. aviation system.

DETROW: We've got about 10 seconds left. Remind us how rare something like this is.

ROSE: Very unusual. This is the second nationwide groundstop since September 11. The most recent was in 2023, and that one only lasted less than 2 hours. So this now appears to be the longest nationwide groundstop since September 11 of 2001.

DETROW: NPR's Joel Rose, thanks so much.

ROSE: You bet.

entries.title: GOP state officials push to revive Trump's mail voting restrictions for 2028 election
entries.summary: Some Republican state officials are reviving a bid for mail-in voting restrictions for the 2028 election by appealing a court order blocking the Postal Service from carrying out a revised ballot rule.
entries.content:
GOP state officials push to revive Trump's mail voting restrictions for 2028 election

Voting for this year's midterm elections just concluded, but Republican officials in a number of states are already looking to shape how votes are cast in 2028.

Twelve GOP state attorneys general are pushing to revive the president's bid for mail-in voting restrictions in time for the 2028 election.

On Thursday, they started the process of appealing a September order by U.S. District Judge Carl Nichols, one of the two judges who blocked the U.S. Postal Service from carrying out a plan released in response to an executive order by President Trump.

The Republican state attorneys general represent Alabama, Florida, Indiana, Kansas, Louisiana, Missouri, Montana, Nebraska, Oklahoma, South Carolina, South Dakota and Texas. It's not clear, however, how long some of these states will continue this case, given that Democrats won up and down the ballot in the midterms. In Texas and Kansas, Democratic candidates are set to take control of their states' attorney general's offices in January.

In September, the Supreme Court refused to pause a similar ruling by U.S. District Judge Indira Talwani, who is based in Boston. That order stopped USPS from working on its revised rule for federal ballot mail, but it only applied to this year's midterm elections.

Nichols' preliminary injunction blocks USPS from implementing the plan for all federal elections, including the 2028 race.

In a court filing, Justice Department attorneys confirmed the Trump administration is not appealing Nichols' ruling. The appeal deadline was Thursday.

The blocked rule — which the Postal Service released in late August — would require states to turn over lists of voters' names and addresses in order to have them delivered by USPS.

Nichols, a Washington, D.C.-based judge who was nominated by Trump, found that the mailing agency likely has no power to impose that requirement on states.

"As the Government concedes, the Postal Service could issue (and enforce) the Rule only if Congress gave it the authority to do so, but here no statute grants the Postal Service the power to issue key parts of the Rule," Nichols wrote.

The administration's earlier push to put these new restrictions in place for the midterms alarmed many election officials, who were concerned about last-minute changes causing major disruptions to the tens of millions who regularly vote by mail. Some voters with disabilities and those in places without polling sites, they feared, could have lost the ability to exercise their right to cast a ballot.

A whistleblower report claimed the online system officials would need to use to follow USPS' revised ballot requirements had not been properly tested and could have resulted in many eligible voters not getting their mail-in ballots in time or at all.

While the Supreme Court ultimately stopped implementation of the USPS rule for the midterms, Justices Samuel Alito and Clarence Thomas dissented from that ruling.

Fellow conservative Justice Brett Kavanaugh said in a concurring opinion that he believed state and local election officials did not have enough time to "reasonably implement the rule" this time. But Kavanaugh noted that "there is at least a fair prospect that the final rule falls within the Postal Service's statutory authority."

Edited by Benjamin Swasey

Correction Nov. 13, 2026

A previous version of this story incorrectly said the deadline for the Justice Department to appeal a court order was Nov. 13. The deadline was Nov. 12.

entries.title: Old tech blamed for the ground stop that caused flight chaos: 'It got overloaded'
entries.summary: The nationwide ground stop that paralyzed the U.S. aviation system on Friday has ended, according to Federal Aviation Administration.
entries.content:
Old tech blamed for the ground stop that caused flight chaos: 'It got overloaded'

The nationwide ground stop that paralyzed the U.S. aviation system on Friday has ended, according to the Federal Aviation Administration.

The rare stop, which lasted about four hours, grounded thousands of flights at all U.S. airports in one of the biggest disruptions of the nation's air travel system since the September 11th attacks.

In a Friday night news conference, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said that air traffic control facilities had experienced "intermittent" outages of their radar and communications systems beginning earlier in the afternoon. Duffy blamed outdated technology for the failures.

"We have old switches, old routers. We use 1980s little copper lines. It's an old system that went down and went down everywhere. It got overloaded," he said.

But when pressed by reporters on exactly why those systems would become overwhelmed on an otherwise normal travel day, Duffy did not have a ready answer.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin joined Duffy in the White House briefing room and said there was no evidence the issue was due to an attack.

"We have seen zero evidence this is a cyber attack," he said.

As of 9 p.m. ET, more than 8,000 flights had been delayed Friday and 7,000 had been canceled in the U.S., according to FlightAware, a flight tracking site. The turmoil comes on the heels of nearly 7,000 flight delays on Thursday.

The FAA said the issue affected Air Route Traffic Control Centers — the regional air traffic control centers across the country that handle high-altitude traffic.

FAA leaders did not brief the media at the White House press conference, and did not provide any further detail on the communication outages that led to the ground stop.

This was only the second nationwide ground stop since September 11, 2001. The U.S. last issued a ground stop of this scale in 2023, when all U.S. airports were shut down due to an outage in the NOTAM (Notice to Air Missions) system, which alerts pilots and airports of real-time hazards.

That outage prompted fears of a cyberattack, but the FAA later determined the issue was caused when contract workers inadvertently deleted critical files.

Senator Richard Blumenthal (D-CT) released a statement late Friday evening calling for a "prompt, penetrating investigation" into the causes of Friday's ground stop.

"A widespread communication outage of this scale is highly alarming — a clear danger to national security, as well as safe, convenient travel close to the holidays. The Department of Transportation owes Americans credible, accurate action and factual disclosure," the statement read.

The FAA has recently begun rolling out an AI-enhanced software tool known as the SMART system as part of its ambitious overhaul of the nation's air traffic control system. But Air Space Intelligence, the company that makes the tool, quickly dismissed speculation that its product could be connected to the flight disruptions.

"The current ground stop is not based on or a result of the SMART system, any product of ASI or our integration with FAA and ATC," the company said on social media.

Passengers stranded

The nationwide ground stop caused chaos in airports and headaches for travelers — many of whom are already too familiar with flight delays and cancellations during the holiday season.

At the Friday night press conference, Duffy said flights would resume but would take time to clear.

At Dallas Fort Worth International Airport, Regina Harling said she waited hours — long past when her flight was supposed to depart — before she learned of the nationwide grounding by checking the news on her phone.

"There's still a sign right in front of me that says we're boarding in 16 minutes," she said Friday afternoon.

Harling needed to travel last minute to San Diego for a family emergency. Stuck at the airport, she said she was thinking about how soon she could make it to her family, but she's not optimistic.

"I was just thinking to myself that it always feels like it's getting harder to travel than it used to be," she said.

At Chicago O'Hare International Airport, Giliann Karon was on board a plane when the ground stop was ordered. Karon said she had already experienced a flight delay the day before due to bad weather in New York City, where she is heading.

"It's just kind of like, 'Oh, of course this is happening,'" she said.

Deepa Shivaram contributed to this report.

entries.title: With his challenge to Schumer, Van Hollen forces a debate over Democrats' mandate
entries.summary: Democrats say they have a mandate to deliver change, but as the party gets ready to retake the majority in both the House and Senate, there are divides over who should lead it.
entries.content:
With his challenge to Schumer, Van Hollen forces a debate over Democrats' mandate

Democrats say they have a mandate to deliver change, but as the party gets ready to retake the majority in both the House and Senate, there are divides over who should lead it.

SACHA PFEIFFER, HOST:

Democrats say they have a mandate to deliver change next year, but as the party gets ready to retake a majority in Congress, there are divides over how far that change should go and who should lead it. It's a debate playing out in the Senate where minority leader Chuck Schumer now faces a challenge from fellow Democrat Chris Van Hollen for the top job next year. Here to break down what we know is NPR's Elena Moore in the studio with me. Hi, Elena.

ELENA MOORE, BYLINE: Hey, Sacha.

PFEIFFER: So last night, Van Hollen announced he's running. For people who don't know him, what should we know about him?

MOORE: Yeah, he's had a pretty long career in Washington, representing Maryland in the Senate since 2017 and serving more than a decade in the House before that, where he held some leadership roles. Ideologically, he's seen as more progressive than Schumer is, and he's tried to position himself in recent years as someone who pushes back hard against the Trump administration. Notably, last year, he lobbied for the release of Kilmar Abrego Garcia, the Maryland man who was wrongly deported to a prison in El Salvador, and Van Hollen actually traveled there to meet with him.

PFEIFFER: And what is Van Hollen's argument for why he should have the Senate's top job?

MOORE: Well, he argues that the midterms showed how much voters want Democrats to reject the status quo. You know, speaking to reporters earlier today at a Democratic conference in Colorado, he argued he's the best person to usher in that change.

(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)

CHRIS VAN HOLLEN: This is about answering the call of the American people because what I'm very afraid of is that their calls to end political corruption, their calls to end a rigged economic system, will require that we organize the Senate in a different way.

MOORE: And, Sacha, those talking points may sound kind of familiar because we kind of just heard them on the campaign trail. Van Hollen is really embracing much of the same messaging used by successful Democratic Senate candidates this cycle, like Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan, who made, you know, their campaigns all about this idea of rejecting the establishment, which, in many ways, Schumer has long embodied.

PFEIFFER: And that message has been successful for some candidates, but...

MOORE: Right.

PFEIFFER: ...In many ways, Van Hollen kind of embodies older school politics. So what makes him think he is an embodiment of change right now?

MOORE: Yeah, and also he's only eight years younger than Schumer, which I think is also kind of important to mention. But it is an important question. On the issues, it's worth noting that he and Schumer are pretty aligned on the party's big-picture priorities. They've both emphasized the need to lower costs, you know, end the war and reverse some of the Trump administration's funding cuts.

I think the bigger difference between the two politicians is how they talk about reforming the Democratic Party. You know, Van Hollen has talked about the Senate being taken over by special interest groups, which hits on a pretty big rift within the caucus right now about campaign donations from super PACs as well as pro-Israel lobbying groups like AIPAC, which is a group that has supported Schumer in the past.

PFEIFFER: And I know that Van Hollen has said he hopes to rally support from the party's left flank. But can you tell if the opposition to Schumer is being driven mainly by progressives, or is there broader appetite for an alternative inside the party?

MOORE: Yeah. It's important to say Schumer is by no means universally loved inside the party, right? You know, towards the start of Trump's second term, he was actually criticized both within the halls of Congress and from voters who argued he wasn't doing enough to fight back against Trump.

Yes, some of that frustration is coming from progressives, like, you know, Vermont Senator Bernie Sanders, for example. But, Sacha, it's not just the party's left flank. You know, earlier this week, Sanders actually held a press conference alongside Elissa Slotkin of Michigan, who's way more of a moderate, I would say. And the two both announced that they wouldn't be backing Schumer for the job.

And, you know, when looking at the broader caucus, dissatisfaction with Schumer may not translate to a victory for Van Hollen, per se, but, you know, he knows he's the underdog here. Schumer says he's confident he has the support needed. But there's also time for both of these politicians to try to make gains. Ultimately, this is going to come down to a secret ballot vote in early December.

PFEIFFER: That is NPR political reporter Elena Moore. Thank you.

MOORE: Thank you.

entries.title: The government says it will close a beloved D.C. park Sunday. Will a judge step in?
entries.summary: Federal judge Ana Reyes grilled the government on Friday about its plans for East Potomac Park, and indicated she could order it to remain open despite President Trump's renovation wishes.
entries.content:
The government says it will close a beloved D.C. park Sunday. Will a judge step in?

Federal judge Ana Reyes grilled the government on Friday about its plans for East Potomac Park, and indicated she could order it to remain open despite President Trump's renovation wishes.

SCOTT DETROW, HOST:

Washington, D.C.'s most beloved parks could close indefinitely on Sunday unless a judge decides to intervene. East Potomac Park is home to the municipal golf course that President Trump wants to redevelop into what he calls a championship-level venue. But at a hearing today, administration lawyers argue that repairs are needed not only to the golf course but to the entire recreational area around it. NPR's Rachel Treisman watched the hearing and joins us now. Hey, Rachel.

RACHEL TREISMAN, BYLINE: Hey, Scott.

DETROW: Did the judge indicate how she'll rule?

TREISMAN: District Judge Ana Reyes sounded like she is likely to take action, but she seemed to be grappling with what exactly she can tell the government to do. The government is arguing it needs to close almost the entire park on Sunday for two main reasons. That's the day the lease expires with the golf course's current operator and because it wants to repair the park's seawall, which has been deteriorating for years. Reyes didn't really seem persuaded by that. The government chose to end its operator lease on November 15, which is the day President Trump has said the park would close. And the government acknowledged it doesn't yet have a plan to repair the seawall or a contract to redevelop the golf course. Reyes suggested she'd rule on Saturday. We'll have to see whether she orders the park to stay open or goes even further and tells the government to keep the golf course open, too.

DETROW: You've been listening to this since 10 in the morning. What are some of the main sticking points from today?

TREISMAN: Yeah. There was a lot of discussion about how Trump's proposed redesign would change a space that so many people here in D.C. just love. Critics say the scale of the course would make it less accessible for beginners, and it would eliminate the perimeter loop that joggers use every day and also for big races, like the Cherry Blossom 10 miler. I spoke to event director Rob Wolfe, who is still hoping the race can take place in April.

ROB WOLFE: It's really important that people understand that if this roadway goes away, hundreds - thousands of people on a daily basis will lose out.

TREISMAN: The government has recently started arguing that the park needs to be closed because the seawall poses a safety issue. At one point, the lawyer mentioned a risk of unattended children falling into the Potomac River at night. The judge seemed pretty incredulous. She kept asking why those concerns hadn't been addressed sooner and whether the whole park really needs to be closed for that.

DETROW: How final are these golf course plans? I mean, all of this seems so up in the air.

TREISMAN: Totally. The government has already submitted this proposal to two different federal commissions, but it still needs to go through environmental reviews and get public input. Reyes has really pressed the government's lawyer on whether it's too late for them to change course, especially given how much people here are opposed to the plan. Reyes says she's gotten death threats over the case. There have been protests by cyclists and birders. At one point, Reyes asked people in the courtroom how many of them were there because they care about East Potomac Park and almost all of them raise their hands.

DETROW: And I think that gets to a bigger storyline here. You know, one reason the case has gotten so much attention is because of the tension between the judge and the government and because of the pointed rulings that the judge has made saying you're not cooperating. Tell us about that.

TREISMAN: Yeah. Reyes has been very vocal about feeling misled by this administration - by officials, by its lawyers. Two weeks ago at the last hearing, she announced she'd open an investigation into potential attorney misconduct, and that there's a long history there with the administration cutting down hundreds of trees in October after telling her they wouldn't, administration officials telling her that there was no final plan to close the course, despite the president saying so online. Reyes has chosen a first-term Trump administration lawyer to lead that probe, but today, the government opposed that, which means Reyes will probably lead that investigation herself.

DETROW: The golf course is, you know, as you've been covering, one of several of these projects that are playing out in court right now. You've got the proposed arch. You've got the Kennedy Center he wants to make the Trump Kennedy Center. What are other possible checks on these projects?

TREISMAN: Well, Democrats have said they hope to use their incoming congressional majority to push back. That could be blocking funding or holding oversight hearings. Judge Reyes actually opened today's hearing by referencing some recent CNN reporting saying the interior department has destroyed documents related to Trump's construction projects, which it denies. Now, Reyes has asked the government's lawyer if he'd heard anything about that. He said, no, and she said if she finds out otherwise, there will be consequences in a zeptosecond. That, she said, is the shortest measurement of time ever recorded in a lab.

DETROW: NPR's Rachel Treisman. Thanks so much.

TREISMAN: Thank you, Scott.

entries.title: What's Trump's strategy now with Iran? To keep things as they are
entries.summary: President Trump says the "status quo" is what Gulf Arab allies want as the Iran war hits a stalemate and the U.S. midterms force a pivot from threats of attacks to economic pressure.
entries.content:
DUBAI, United Arab Emirates — President Trump is confronting new realities nine months into the war with Iran that leave him with dwindling options to ending the conflict.

On Thursday, he waved away the need for a deal with Iran, saying the U.S. has billions of Iran's dollars frozen in overseas accounts.

"We don't need a deal with Iran. Those days have long since passed. We've got their money," he wrote in a Truth Social post.

Negotiations with Iran are stuck with mediator Qatar working to bridge the divide. Trump met Qatar's prime minister at the White House this week, and said afterward that Gulf Arab allies prefer "the status quo" of continued economic pressure on Iran. He wrote that while the U.S. remains "locked and loaded," an attack at this point "seems to be quite unlikely."

That's a pivot from his threats to carry out quick, intense strikes on Iran in the days before he had to contend with two election setbacks.

Trump's wartime ally, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, whom he'd thrown his support behind, is on the cusp of being ousted from power after elections there.

Meanwhile, at home, Trump's party lost its majority in Congress in midterm elections. Vice President Vance blamed Republican losses on the unpopular war with Iran and the nature of U.S. relations with Israel.

With less room to room maneuver and Iran still defiant, Trump's strategy appears to be to keep things as they are, for now. That means the possibility of escalation still looms.

Senior UAE diplomat, Anwar Gargash, told an audience in the country's capital of Abu Dhabi this week that the region must "prepare for a prolonged period of uncertainty, in which neither a decisive resolution nor a stable regional order can be taken for granted."

Here's what keeping the status quo looks like.

Iran's chokehold on the Strait of Hormuz persists

Official Iranian social media accounts frequently post videos of attacks on ships in the Strait of Hormuz for violating Iran's new rules requiring permission to navigate the waterway, which was open and free to ships before the war.

The U.S., meanwhile, is assisting oil tankers through the Strait of Hormuz using a route that's close to Oman's coastline. While this has helped Arab states export their oil, it does not solve the bigger problem of how to bring back the pre-war production levels of other vital products like liquified natural gas, fertilizer and aluminum. Nor does a status quo allow countries like Kuwait, Qatar and Bahrain to import goods to their ports.

The International Monetary Fund says Gulf Arab states are in economic recession as a result of the war, despite higher oil prices. It says Kuwait, Qatar and Iraq's economies are contracting approximately 16% this year. Bahrain's is down 11%.

More limited strikes that could rapidly escalate

The U.S. is sending a third aircraft carrier with thousands of troops to the region, leaving open the possibility of another planned military escalation.

This week, Iran unveiled what it says is a new underground missile production site.

The U.S. and Iran are also still occasionally carrying out tit-for-tat for strikes.

On Friday, Iranian media said the U.S. struck one of its islands in the Strait of Hormuz. It's an area where Iran has radars and drone launch sites. Iran's Revolutionary Guard said it hit back, targeting an early warning U.S. radar in Bahrain.

Iran remains economically battered, starved of oil revenue

Secretary of State Marco Rubio told reporters this week there's no need for military action against Iran at this stage because economic sanctions are doing the job.

"The pain that they're feeling is, eventually you have to eat. Eventually you have to be able to pay your own fighters and your own security forces," Rubio said.

There's also a U.S. naval blockade at sea barring Iranian ships from transporting oil to countries like China. This blockade, according to the U.S. military, has cut Iran off from at least $25 billion in revenue so far.

One of the biggest economic blows, though, has come from the United Arab Emirates. The UAE announced over the summer it was severing all economic and trade ties with Iran. The UAE had been among Iran's biggest trade partners and local bank accounts were allegedly used by Iran's supreme leader and Revolutionary Guard to move money around.

Meanwhile, the U.S. military's Central Command announced a new operation, dubbed "Iron Gate," with other U.S. government agencies, aimed at preventing Iran from using land routes to transport advanced weapons across its borders and the Caspian Sea.

War in Yemen intensifies, draws in more countries

Another consequence of the conflict with Iran is the resumption of all-out war between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis in Yemen.

The Houthis, who are not a direct proxy of Iran but are supported by it, say Saudi airstrikes across Yemen have killed scores of people in past months, including nearly 60 this past weekend, many of them women and children in a village near the capital Sana'a.

Saudi Arabia, meanwhile, faces daily missile and drone attacks by Houthis, including some this week that hit its key East-West pipeline carrying crude oil to bypass the Strait of Hormuz. Another Houthi attack hit Saudi oil company Aramco's skyscraper headquarters in Riyadh's financial district.

Deadly Houthi attacks on Saudi airports have led to flights and high-profile events being canceled.

As the Yemen war drags on, Pakistan, Turkey and Egypt are among the countries entering the fray with defensive support to Saudi Arabia. The U.S. is assisting with intelligence on the Houthis.

The United Nations says some 330,000 Yemenis have been displaced by the renewed fighting between the Houthis and the Saudi-backed Yemeni government, exacerbating an already dire humanitarian crisis.

Efforts by mediators continue, neither side budges

Iran says it's prepared for a short-term pause on attacks on ships in the Strait of Hormuz, but insists that seven demands be met before entering into direct talks over its nuclear program.

"The message has been only one thing. These seven items are on the table. Take it or leave it," Hamidreza Gholamzade, Tehran municipality spokesperson, told NPR.

These demands include lifting sanctions, ending the naval blockade, unfreezing Iran's dollars in overseas accounts and enforcing a ceasefire across all fronts, which includes halting Israeli attacks in Lebanon and Gaza.

Rubio has described the conditions as "absurd."

There's also discussion on diluting and moving Iran's enriched uranium abroad. However, the head of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, Mohsen Rezaei, told Iran's state broadcaster Wednesday: "We will not remove even a shred of enriched nuclear material from Iran."

It's another indication of the gridlock.

NPR's Hadeel Al-Shalchi in Antalya, Turkey, and Ahmed Abu Hamada in Cairo contributed reporting.

entries.title: The Trump administration's voter roll crusade could continue
entries.summary: Election officials are preparing for the Trump administration's pressure tactics over potential noncitizens on state voter rolls to continue, though recent court rulings pose new obstacles.
entries.content:
The Trump administration's voter roll crusade could continue

In the weeks before Election Day, the Trump administration escalated its hunt for voter fraud and its pressure on election officials — especially in California — to crack down on illegal voting by non-U.S. citizens.

Now, with Election Day come and gone, election officials and civil rights attorneys are preparing for the administration to continue its search for noncitizens on state voter rolls, as well as what they see as intimidation tactics toward election officials.

"It's clear that there is this drive to try to conjure up facts that just don't exist. I don't think that's going to change," James Williams, county executive for California's Santa Clara County, told NPR. "So we fully are prepared to continue to deal with this."

In recent weeks, federal prosecutors announced criminal charges against dozens of people who are accused of voting or registering to vote without being a citizen. Yet compared to overall numbers of voters, noncitizen voting is exceptionally rare. And since summer, the administration has touted what turned out to be grossly inflated numbers of noncitizens on state voter rolls.

In mid-October, federal officials alleged they had found 20,000 "likely" noncitizens on California's voter rolls. The Department of Justice sued the state to try to force election officials not to count ballots of voters whose citizenship had not been verified. A federal judge and a federal appeals court rejected the DOJ's requests, and the U.S. Supreme Court declined to intervene.

In the days leading up to Election Day, with the lawsuit pending, U.S. attorneys in California sent grand jury subpoenas to several counties, asking for records related to how local officials responded to DOJ's demands.

Though DOJ dropped its lawsuit last week, it has not rescinded these subpoenas.

"We have ongoing cases and investigations in various states surrounding voter process," U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche said at a Thursday press conference. "We are actively, and will continue to investigate election integrity cases criminally and civilly, and that wasn't expected to start or stop — no matter what the results of the election were last week."

But recent unfavorable rulings for the Trump administration have created new obstacles for future federal attempts to intervene on state voter list maintenance.

"Do I think they will still keep at this? I do, but there are just a lot of court losses that are going to be really difficult for them to maneuver around," Anna Baldwin, director of voting rights litigation at Campaign Legal Center, told NPR. "They've hit substantial roadblocks because it's a lawless program that Congress has never authorized."

Recent court orders reaffirmed that states have the authority to run their elections and called into question the credibility of the federal government's data on noncitizens.

One key ruling, which came down the night before Election Day, found that DOJ and the Department of Homeland Security lack any statutory authority to distribute lists of purported noncitizens to election officials. In that order, a federal judge in Washington, D.C., wrote that taking that action also violates the Privacy Act. The federal government could appeal.

In an earlier order in October, a different D.C.-based judge vacated the DOJ's project of requesting unredacted voter rolls from states, seeking to compare that voter data to federal databases, and instructing states to remove suspected noncitizens. The ruling found those actions were unlawful and disenfranchised eligible voters. The DOJ has appealed.

The Department of Justice declined to comment on litigation or future plans, but said in a statement, "The Department will continue to enforce federal election laws and will evaluate matters based on the facts and the law."

Looming criminal proceedings and subpoenas to election officials

Federal prosecutors have vowed to continue tracking down noncitizen voting cases, as have some local prosecutors. San Luis Obispo District Attorney Dan Dow is investigating the potential noncitizen voters federal officials flagged in his county. He has so far charged one individual.

"It has always been a crime but I've never had a noncitizen case referred to me. When we got 63 of them, we said, 'We will look at them,'" Dow told NPR. "It is our duty to uphold California law."

Loyola Law School professor Justin Levitt, who was a White House adviser on voting rights in the Biden administration, said he expects "a trickle of actual follow-through on actual cases" of noncitizens voting. "And that is also entirely consistent with everything we knew for decades — which is that this does happen, but it doesn't happen very often."

What remains to be seen is whether the Justice Department will retreat from the criminal threats federal officials have waged against local election officials, or try to escalate those further.

In letters delivered to every California county in October, DOJ officials warned: "If persons knowingly tabulate ballots cast by individuals identified by federal agencies as noncitizens, they risk becoming aiders and abettors to a federal crime."

President Trump added on Truth Social: "They will all go to jail for a long period of time!!!"

In the days before Election Day, officials in Los Angeles County as well as Bay Area counties, including Santa Clara and Sonoma, received subpoenas from their local U.S. attorney's office to turn over records this month.

In Sonoma, the subpoena is for records about an individual the DOJ alleges may have voted in a past election without being a U.S. citizen, as well as records about how county officials responded to DOJ requests to segregate ballots of people on its list of possible noncitizens, according to Sonoma County Counsel Joshua Myers.

The Oct. 21 subpoena sent to Los Angeles County, which was reviewed by NPR, requests records related to how the registrar-recorder's office screens for unlawful voting by noncitizens, as well as records responding to federal correspondence, including the demand to segregate ballots.

The DOJ said it does not comment on alleged subpoenas. But the substance of the subpoenas has raised questions about whether there may be a criminal probe targeted at counties.

Williams of Santa Clara County declined to speak about the subpoenas but said criminal threats against government employees who are trying to lawfully administer elections "strikes at the heart of what it means to live in a free society."

Looking forward, Williams said he is hoping for a way to productively collaborate with the federal government again.

"We should be aligned — federal, state and local government — in facilitating every citizen exercising their right to vote. And of course, we want voter rolls that don't include noncitizens," he said. "There's no disagreement about that."

Inflated and inaccurate lists

Another hurdle for the federal government's efforts to publicize purported noncitizens on voter rolls is the inaccuracies in its tallies so far.

Trump claimed in July there were 250,000 noncitizens registered in four states, including in California. But state officials pushed back on the data, and federal officials admitted the earlier numbers were a "ceiling" of potential noncitizens. In mid-October, federal officials had sent California its list of 20,000 "likely" noncitizens registered to vote in the state.

The federal government has never maintained a complete list of U.S. citizens. Trump administration efforts to cobble together citizenship data from various sources have led to naturalized citizens being mistakenly flagged as noncitizens, and data experts have warned the federal government's methodology in California was likely to also lead to false matches.

The weekend before Election Day, a federal judge allowed data experts from University of California Los Angeles' Voting Rights Project to analyze the DOJ's list of 20,000 names. The analysis found 42% did not appear on California's current voter roll and that naturalized citizens were on the list.

Separately, several California counties have noted the lists from DOJ were riddled with duplicates and obvious inaccuracies.

Santa Cruz County's top election official, Tricia Webber, wrote in an email that of the 81 people DOJ had listed as suspected noncitizens registered to vote in her county, "more than half are not registered in Santa Cruz County; some names do not match any person currently registered or previously registered," and some dates of birth "were wildly inaccurate with some dates appearing well into the future like 2044."

Even DOJ attorneys acknowledged in court hearings under questioning from judges that there have been flaws with federal lists of likely noncitizens.

U.S. District Judge David Carter, a Clinton nominee, who was presiding over the federal government's lawsuit against California, had planned to hold proceedings that would assess the accuracy of DOJ's lists. That will no longer happen since the DOJ dropped its lawsuit.

For Loyola Law School's Levitt, questions remain about whether federal officials violated the Privacy Act by using California voter roll data for this project without following required public notice procedures.

And with Democrats winning control of Congress, lawmakers could hold hearings that probe deeper into how federal officials came up with their list, said David Becker, the executive director for the Center for Election Innovation and Research.

"I think we're going to have some very serious scrutiny of the Department of Homeland Security and their methodology as they assisted the administration in its failed effort to try to demonstrate there was widespread noncitizen voting in this country," Becker said.

entries.title: Does Europe regret its bet on U.S. defense?
entries.summary: Europe bet big on American defense technology and they're now paying the price. Years-long backlogs are underway due to production delays and the U.S. own military needs.
entries.content:
Does Europe regret its bet on U.S. defense?

You're reading a newsletter from The Indicator from Planet Money. Once a week, we curate our favorite stories and insights on business, finance, economics and why they matter. Subscribe here to get it in your inbox every Friday.

Fox has officially acquired Roku and there are CONSEQUENCES. For one, the "Marine Aquarium" screensaver will no longer be available. One person posted on the "Mildly Infuriating" subreddit: "I can't believe it I love my fish what am I gunna do."

The artist behind that screensaver, Jim Sachs, is NOT renewing his license due to Fox's acquisition. "It seems that Fox simply wants another venue for spreading their philosophy, which I consider repugnant. I can't stand the idea of my artwork being used to lure even one person down that rabbit hole," Sachs told Ars Technica. The licensing deal will have big personal consequences for Sachs, who relies on the $80,000 per year licensing deal. Another comment on the subreddit posted, "This is the last straw, Apple TV for me."

Coming up

  • The U.S. can't keep up with defense demand
  • How housing affects fertility rates in Spain
  • What Walmart stock has to do with the economy

News We're Watching

Did Europe make a bad bet on American defense tech? - Bruegel

What to Know: Over the past decade, European countries have become increasingly reliant on U.S. technology to support their air defense systems. We're talking fighter jets & missile defense systems like the Patriot, which can intercept ballistic missiles. It seemed like an obvious choice: these are high-quality pieces of technology, they're readily available, and buying American keeps the U.S. committed to European defense. Here's the problem: the whole "readily available" thing doesn't seem to be true. There is a MAJOR backlog of missiles while demand just keeps going up. That's due to both production delays and the U.S.' own military needs in Iran. PLUS!! European countries that bought technology like the Patriot are now locked in to American equipment. They can't just switch to another supplier to get missiles.

Why this matters: You kind of want to know if you're not gonna get a few hundred missiles on time. While the U.S. is focused on the Iran war, threats from Russia still loom large in Europe. And now, many European nations are at the whim of these defense contracts panning out… having to put up with delays and higher costs. The article's authors look back and see a missed opportunity in 2022 for investment into homegrown systems: "Calls to Europeanise the funding and ordering of air defense systems were ignored and the strategic gap is now all too visible."

Business journalist and friend of the show Paddy Hirsch adds: "No one could have predicted the extent to which Trump would damage the relationship between the U.S. and Europe. But the fact is that Trump isn't the first president to beat the drum about European over-dependence on the US. He's just the first to really force the issue. And guess what? He was doing Europe a favor! Europe desperately needs to wean itself off the U.S. teat, and not just because of the unpredictability of a Presidential whim. But because there's no telling how U.S. and European interests will diverge over the next few decades."

Could more housing lead to a higher fertility rate? - Elcano Royal Institute

What to Know: Spain has one of the lowest fertility rates in the world. It's currently at 1.1, meaning 100 women birth 110 children on average. To maintain the current population, rates would need to sit at 2.1. Immigration has kept the population from dropping dramatically since 2000, but the author offers a DIFFERENT solution to Spain's childbearing woes: more housing. Spain, like many countries, has struggled with expensive housing: prices have risen 81% between 2015 to 2025. The average age of leaving the parental home in Spain is 30.2 compared to 23.8 in France and 24.1 in Germany. The author asks: could an influx of public housing incentivize partners to start families earlier?

How realistic is this?: There's no hard evidence in the Elcano article showing more housing actually leads to a higher fertility rate. That said, Planet Money co-host Jeff Guo says the evidence for this argument does look stronger outside the U.S. There was literally a paper about this topic IN SPAIN that came out a few weeks ago. The paper found a 10% rise in local housing prices LOWERS birth rates by about 3% for women 20-34. In fact, the authors deduced that higher housing prices account for roughly HALF of the 2014-2022 implied fertility rate decline. In short: more expensive housing = fewer kids.

Today's Indicator

The stock market might be the economy… just ask Walmart

If you HAVEN'T listened: We all know the old adage "the stock market doesn't equal the economy." Well, lately, maybe it does!! At least more than usual. The "new era" economy (AI, tech etc.) has an outsized impact on the growth of both the stock market AND economic growth. That's all well and good, except hyper-concentration means hyper-risk. If AI stocks start to tumble, it could have a negative chain reaction on the economy in a uniquely problematic way. Two non-profits in the episode warn that the AI bubble is a thing. In short, the economy depends on the market! A downturn there is more likely to mean an economic downturn too. Diversification is important, people.

If you HAVE listened: You know that the economic risk isn't just about a market downturn. It's about the impacts that follow. Consumer spending is driving much of economic growth, and that's led by wealthy spenders. Another downstream risk: pension funds hold debt related to the AI buildout, according to the report from the Open Markets Institute and Americans for Financial Reform Education Fund. They argue this has exposed pension funds and even ordinary workers to dangerous risk! Reporter Wailin Wong says, "That's something I wasn't able to get into in the episode, since we were focused on stocks and not debt. But certainly the credit markets are a huge part of this story too."

REST OF THE WEEK

  • The winners and losers of the Midterm Elections
  • Mike Schur and the Case of the Missing Sitcom
  • Why public schools are adding personal finance classes

In Our Spare Time

Reporter Ricky Mulvey read A Violent Masterpiece

It's a profane, no-holds-barred thriller. Jordan Harper wrote on TV shows in Hollywood before getting disillusioned with the industry and writing about some of its seedier parts in novels.

A Violent Masterpiece follows three storylines that converge around a suspicious death in a jail cell. It's Eyes Wide Shut meets LA Confidential.

Two things I really admire about Harper's work.

  • It's confidently modern. I think a lot of writers find more comfort writing about the distant past and allowing readers to find parallels to today. A Violent Masterpiece is confident and planted in the right now.
  • Harper's razor-sharp writing style. He cut his teeth writing for television, so his work is well-structured and every word counts.

A Violent Masterpiece is a perfect book to rip through on a plane if you are traveling for the holidays. A genteel reader should stay far away, and sickos should pick it up. The story is far from perfect; you'll see why at the ending. I loved it.
